claims.proposition_evaluated: The $100 million approved for capital profile CM-20-0330 (Active Transportation Implementation Acceleration - Approach 3, 2023-2026) is almost double (ratio at least 1.8) the City of Edmonton's annual Snow and Ice Control gross expenditure budget, primary denominator the approved 2022 gross budget, alternative the approved 2023 gross budget.
claims.interpretation_notes: MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN. The brief fixes the primary denominator as 'the approved 2022 gross Snow and Ice Control expenditure budget, the annual budget in force when the statement was captured'. The public record holds two different 'approved 2022' gross figures and the verdict word flips between them. (1) The base annual budget: the Approved 2019-2022 Operating Budget, Parks and Roads Services branch summary by program (PDF p.209, printed p.205, $000s), shows Snow and Ice Control net expenditure and transfers of 63,666 for 2022 (revenue and transfers 13). Ratio 100,000/63,666 = 1.571, Partially supported under both cutoff sets. (2) The budget in force on 2022-12-12 as amended in-year: the Operating Financial Update - December 31, 2022 (FCS01656, Attachment 1, supplemental table p.38 of 45, $000s) prints Snow and Ice Control Budget: Revenue 23,108, Expense 79,474, Net Position (56,366), with no COVID adjustment column entries; the 2022 Budget Highlights (p.101) records that Council added $14.3 million one-time from the Financial Stabilization Reserve at the Spring 2022 adjustment for the enhanced snow-clearing pilot, and CO01733 records a further one-time $4.7 million on 2022-07-04. So about $19 million of the 79,474 is one-time reserve-funded top-up after a severe winter, which is why the 2022 revenue line (23,108) is ten times the 2023-2025 revenue lines (2,401; 2,143; 967). Ratio 100,000/79,474 = 1.258: Contradicted under the primary cutoffs, Partially supported under the alternative cutoffs (1.25 threshold, by 0.008). 'In force' points to reading (2); 'the City's annual snow-clearing budget' in ordinary speech points to reading (1). The framing I would use: the base approved annual budget excluding one-time in-year additions (reading 1), with the amended figure and the net tax-levy figure reported beside it; or the brief should say explicitly that in-year one-time additions count. I answer under reading (1) because it is the 'approved' annual budget a resident would find in the budget book and because the amended figure is dominated by one-time money; the classification under reading (2) is reported here so synthesis can substitute it. Alternative denominator, 2023 approved gross: the Parks and Roads Services Annual Service Plan 2022/2023, Appendix A Financial Summary, '2023 BUDGET (000s)': Snow and Ice Control Expenses 62,288, Recovery (1,128), Revenue (63), Net 61,097. Ratio 1.605, Partially supported under both cutoff sets. The Operating Financial Update - December 31, 2023 (FCS02229, Attachment 1 supplemental table) prints the 2023 year-end budget as Expense 63,574, Revenue 2,401, Net (61,173); ratio 1.573, also Partially supported. Net tax-levy 2022 (56,366): ratio 1.774, Partially supported under primary cutoffs, Supported under alternative cutoffs (at least 1.7). Under every reading the failing part of the proposition is the word 'double': no published annual figure gives a ratio of 1.8 or more, and the highest (1.77) is the 2022 net figure. The holder's page gives no figure and no source, so nothing establishes that it used the proposed 2023 figure. The CM-20-0330 figure is confirmed from the profile sheet (Capital Budget p.540-543, $000s: 5,950 / 26,750 / 33,650 / 33,650 = 100,000, Tax-Supported Debt, Service Category blank) and the council minutes (Capital Budget Amendment 7 as re-stated, Carried 9 to 4). No constant-dollar restatement was applied.

limitations: Verdict figure and classifications ($000s, nominal): primary denominator, base approved 2022 gross 63,666 -> ratio 1.571 -> Partially supported (primary cutoffs) / Partially supported (alternative cutoffs). Same denominator read as the 2022 budget in force at year-end, 79,474 -> 1.258 -> Contradicted (primary) / Partially supported (alternative). Alternative denominator, approved 2023 gross 62,288 -> 1.605 -> Partially supported / Partially supported; 2023 year-end budget 63,574 -> 1.573 -> Partially supported / Partially supported. The finding is definition-sensitive only if the amended 2022 figure is used.
Net tax-levy ratio (qualification 3): 2022 net budget 56,366 -> 1.774 -> Partially supported (primary) / Supported (alternative); 2023 net 61,097 -> 1.637 -> Partially supported under both.

Like-for-like (qualification 1a), approved CM-20-0330 allocation against the same year's snow budget: 2023 5,950 / 62,288 = 0.096; 2024 26,750 / 67,090 = 0.399; 2025 33,650 / 67,554 = 0.498; 2026 33,650 / 68,500 (CO01733 figure) = 0.491. Approved average 25,000 per year against snow budgets of 62,288-68,500 = about 0.37-0.40.

Like-for-like (qualification 1b), whole $100,000 against four years of snow budgets 62,288 + 67,090 + 67,554 + 68,500 = 265,432 -> 0.377 (using the 2023 year-end budget 63,574 instead: 266,718 -> 0.375). The 2024 and 2025 figures are year-end budgets after in-year adjustments; the 2026 figure is the December 2022 approval as stated in CO01733, since the 2026 Approved Operating Budget document prints no Snow and Ice Control line.

Actuals (qualification 2), from cumulative CM-20-0330 'To-Date Actuals' in the Capital Financial Updates: 807 at 2023-12-31; 10,496 at 2024-12-31; 25,093 at 2025-09-30; 39,984 at 2025-12-31. Yearly: 2023 = 807; 2024 = 10,496 - 807 = 9,689; 2025 = 39,984 - 10,496 = 29,488; total spent to 2025-12-31 = 39,984 (40.2 per cent of the amended 99,570; 40.0 per cent of 100,000); actual average 2023-2025 = 13,328 per year. Against snow actual expenditure: 2023 807 / 54,917 = 0.015; 2024 9,689 / 72,086 = 0.134; 2025 29,488 / 76,648 = 0.385. 2022 snow actual (context only) 97,571 -> $100M is 1.025 times it.

The 2019-2022 budget's 2022 column was set in December 2018 and could have been altered by the Fall 2021 adjustment that fixed the 2022 budget; the 2022 Budget Highlights show only branch-level changes, so a small difference from 63,666 in the budget approved in December 2021 cannot be excluded. The 2022 year-end 'Budget' column shows no adjustment entries for Snow and Ice Control, so the 79,474 figure is the in-force budget including the one-time additions.

The 2023 Snow and Ice Control figure in the service plan (62,288) is labelled '2023 BUDGET' but the plan's publication date is not printed; the year-end 2023 budget (63,574) includes any 2023 in-year adjustments. Either gives the same classification.

Attachment 2 to CO01733 (the brief's named source) is an unlabelled chart by winter season; its approximate bar heights (about $57-58M base, rising to about $67M by 2025-26) are consistent with the figures used but were not used for any ratio.

The 2023-2026 Operating Budget document publishes Snow and Ice Control only inside the Parks and Roads Services branch totals (2022 adjusted expenditure 227,146; 2023 232,498, $000s) and in the enhancement service package; it does not print a program-level snow budget, so the operative figures come from the branch service plan and the City's year-end financial updates.

The affordable-housing comparison on the same page was not tested; for context, council's minutes record Amendment 6 increasing profile 19-90-4100 Affordable Housing Land Acquisition by $91,700,000 (2023-2026) and CBC/Global reported $22.9 million for 2023; the page does not say which figure it compared against.
unknowns: Which figure, if any, the holder used as 'the City's annual snow-clearing budget'; the page names none. A denominator of about $52-55 million would be needed for 'almost double' at the 1.8 threshold, and no published annual budget figure is that low except the 2022 net tax-levy figure (56,366) at 1.77.
The exact Snow and Ice Control budget for 2022 as approved in December 2021 (program level), and how much of the 2022 year-end revenue line of 23,108 is reserve transfer versus recoveries.
Whether any 2026 in-year adjustment changed the 2026 Snow and Ice Control budget from the $68.5 million approved in December 2022 (the Spring 2026 adjustment was not located).

claims.suggested_one_line: $100 million is about 1.5 to 1.6 times a year's approved snow-and-ice budget (roughly $62-64 million in 2022 and 2023), well above it but not 'almost double'; only the 2022 net tax-levy figure gets close (1.77), and against the 2022 budget as topped up after that winter it is only 1.26 times.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Council approved $100 million for the bike-network program (profile CM-20-0330) over 2023-2026. The City's approved Snow and Ice Control budget was $63.7 million for 2022 (base budget) and $62.3 million for 2023, so $100 million is about 1.6 times one year of snow clearing, not double. The 2022 budget actually in force by December 2022 had been topped up with about $19 million of one-time money, to $79.5 million, which makes the ratio 1.26. On the 2022 net tax-levy figure ($56.4 million) the ratio is 1.77. Like for like, the program's average $25 million a year is about 0.4 of a year's snow budget, and its actual spending was $0.8 million in 2023, $9.7 million in 2024 and $29.5 million in 2025 against snow spending of $54.9 million, $72.1 million and $76.6 million.
suggested_tldr: $100 million approved for bike-network profile CM-20-0330, 2023-2026, approved 2022-12-09 by a 9-4 vote.
Approved snow-and-ice budget: $63.7M (2022 base), $62.3M (2023); ratio about 1.6, not 1.8.
2022 budget as amended in-year was $79.5M (ratio 1.26); 2022 net tax levy $56.4M (ratio 1.77).
Per year, the program averages $25M against $62-69M of snow budget; spent $40.0M by end of 2025.

claims.proposition_evaluated: In the City's 2023-2026 capital budget as adopted in December 2022, roads get $1.8 billion, about eighteen times the $100 million for bike lanes; verdict figure is the 2023-2026 approved total of profiles with Service Category 'Roads' or 'Neighbourhood Renewal' plus the three vehicle-carrying bridge profiles, less the two predeclared exclusions.
claims.interpretation_notes: Quotation discrepancy: the Global News report of 2022-12-12 quotes Councillor Janz as saying 'Only $100 million is going to bike lanes but $1.8 billion, 180 times as much, is going towards roads.' $1.8 billion is 18 times $100 million, not 180. No other record of the statement was found: the council minutes record motions and votes, not debate speech; Global News's 2022-12-09 article, CBC's 2022-12-09 article and Taproot's 2022-12-12 article do not carry the quotation; council meeting video was not reviewed. The figure appears only as '180' in the one record found. Source of the $1.8 billion: Table 8 of the adopted Capital Budget gives 'Active Pathways and Roads Service' at $1,794.0 million for 2023-2026, which rounds to $1.8 billion; that line includes CM-20-0330 itself and the other active-pathway profiles, so the councillor's figure appears to be the combined service line, not a roads-only total. Membership check against the profile sheets: every profile in the editor's reading carries the stated label (18 'Roads' profiles, 11 'Neighbourhood Renewal' profiles); the three bridges (23-24-0300, 21-24-9301, 21-24-9302) carry no Service Category; the two exclusions 21-20-2100 and 14-66-2570 do carry 'Roads' as the brief says. One label differs from the brief's description of the widest reading: 21-50-9100 103A Avenue Pedway carries Service Category 'Economic Development', not a blank; the other five widest-reading profiles are blank. CM-20-0330's own sheet has a blank Service Category. Two blank-category transportation profiles sit outside every reading: CM-29-0000 Transportation - Minor Renewal Program (15,000) and 21-31-9100 Rundle Park Road and Parking Lot Renewal (181). Results ($000s): primary roads-only total 1,945,703 = $1.946 billion, ratio 19.46 -> Supported under both cutoff sets (at least 1.5B; at least 1.62B). Required alternative, 'Active Pathways and Roads Service' 1,794.0 million, ratio 17.94 -> Supported under both, reported as the combined service allocation, not a roads total. Widest 2,025,848 (ratio 20.26) -> Supported; narrowest (Service Category 'Roads' only) 1,116,532 (ratio 11.17) -> Partially supported under both sets. The finding is not definition-sensitive between the primary and the required alternative; it becomes Partially supported only on the narrowest reading, which drops Neighbourhood Renewal (722,289) and the bridges (106,882).

claims.suggested_one_line: On the City's own profile labels, roads and neighbourhood-renewal profiles total about $1.95 billion in the adopted 2023-2026 capital budget, about 19 times the $100 million bike program; the councillor's '$1.8 billion' matches the combined 'Active Pathways and Roads' line, which itself contains the bike money, and '180 times' should be 18.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Adding every 2023-2026 capital profile the City labels 'Roads' or 'Neighbourhood Renewal', plus three vehicle bridges, gives $1,945.7 million, 19.5 times the $100 million for profile CM-20-0330. The combined 'Active Pathways and Roads Service' line in Table 8 is $1,794.0 million (17.9 times), but it includes the bike program and other pathway projects. Counting only profiles labelled 'Roads' gives $1,116.5 million, 11.2 times. The councillor's '180 times' is an arithmetic slip; $1.8 billion is 18 times $100 million. Since adoption the bike profile has been cut by $430,000 (June 2025) and had spent $40.0 million by the end of 2025; several road profiles have grown, so the ratio today would differ.
suggested_tldr: Roads-only profiles (City labels, incl. Neighbourhood Renewal and three bridges): $1,945.7M, 19.5 times $100M.
Combined 'Active Pathways and Roads Service' line: $1,794.0M, includes the bike program itself.
Quote says '180 times'; $1.8B is 18 times $100M. CM-20-0330 amended to $99.57M in June 2025; $40.0M spent to end-2025.
